title: The least-squares line
caption: The five toy rows from the notes. The dashed red sticks are the residuals — the vertical distance between what happened and what the model says. Least squares picks the one line out of infinitely many that makes the sum of those sticks, squared, as small as possible. It is a definition, not a guess.

title: Why we square the errors
caption: Each residual is drawn as a literal square, so its area is the squared error. Least squares minimises the total shaded area. Squaring stops positive and negative misses from cancelling, and punishes one big miss far more than several small ones — which is exactly why the fitted line refuses to ignore an outlier.

title: The loss surface is a bowl
caption: Fix the data, vary the two parameters, and plot the resulting MSE. The surface is a convex bowl with exactly one bottom. That single fact is why linear regression has a closed-form answer and why gradient descent on it can never get stuck in a bad local minimum — there are no other minima to get stuck in.

title: Gradient descent: rolling downhill
caption: Instead of solving for the answer, start anywhere and repeatedly step against the slope of the loss. Each arrow is one update of w and b. It converges to the exact same point the closed-form formula gives — it must, because the bowl has one bottom. This matters because most models have no closed form, and this loop is all they have.

title: The learning rate decides everything
caption: One knob, three completely different outcomes. Too small and you burn compute crawling toward the answer. Too large and each step overshoots the valley, bouncing to ever-worse parameters until the loss blows up. The useful range is wide but not unlimited — and this same knob reappears in XGBoost as the shrinkage applied to every tree.

title: Why features get standardised
caption: Left: on raw prices the loss valley is a long thin ravine, because w and b are measured in wildly different units. Gradient descent zigzags across the ravine instead of running along it, and you must use a tiny step size to avoid diverging. Right: after centring and scaling, the valley is nearly circular and the path goes almost straight to the bottom.

title: Underfitting and overfitting
caption: The same data fitted with a straight line, a gentle curve and a wildly flexible curve. Degree 1 is too rigid to follow the real shape (high bias). Degree 15 threads every single training point, including the noise, and goes haywire between them (high variance). Degree 4 recovers the underlying truth. Note that the *training* error keeps falling the whole time — which is precisely why training error must never be your judge.

title: The bias–variance trade-off
caption: Sweep model flexibility and track two errors. Training error falls forever — more flexibility can always fit the data you already have. Test error falls, bottoms out, then climbs as the model starts memorising noise it will never see again. The gap between the two curves *is* overfitting, and the bottom of the test curve is the model you want.

title: Ridge shrinks, Lasso selects
caption: Six features, only two of which genuinely drive demand; the rest are noise. As the penalty λ grows, Ridge pulls every coefficient smoothly toward zero but never quite lets go of any of them. Lasso drives the useless ones to exactly zero, one after another, and keeps the real signal longest — that is automatic feature selection falling out of the penalty's shape.

title: Why L1 produces exact zeros
caption: The ellipses are contours of squared error, centred on the unpenalised solution. The penalty confines the answer to the shaded region, so the fit lands where the smallest affordable ellipse first touches that region. L2's region is a circle — contact almost always happens off-axis, so both weights stay non-zero. L1's region is a diamond with corners *on* the axes, and corners are what an expanding ellipse hits first.
